claims.text: A nanoscale Ag interlayer at W–Cu interfaces will increase the overall thermal conductivity of the composite.
The Ag-modified composite will retain mechanical durability under fusion-reactor joint operating conditions.
The Ag-modified composite will retain irradiation resistance under fusion-reactor joint operating conditions.
The baseline is a W–Cu composite in which tungsten and copper are directly bonded without interfacial modification.
Coating tungsten surfaces with nanoscale Ag before consolidation will create an Ag interlayer at the W–Cu interfaces.
Fusion-reactor joint service involves high temperature, high heat flux, irradiation, and thermal cycling.
Silver has exceptionally high intrinsic thermal conductivity.
Silver has excellent wetting with tungsten.
Silver has excellent wetting with copper.
The Ag interlayer will reduce W–Cu interfacial thermal resistance.
The Ag interlayer will promote better metallurgical bonding across the W–Cu interface.
The Ag interlayer will improve electron transport across the W–Cu interface.
Keeping the Ag interlayer very thin will prevent the introduction of deleterious phases.
A very thin Ag interlayer will not compromise the mechanical integrity of the W–Cu composite.
A very thin Ag interlayer will not compromise the irradiation resistance of the W–Cu composite.
Relative to unmodified W–Cu, the Ag-coated composite will retain comparable mechanical strength and irradiation-damage tolerance.
The beneficial effect requires a nanoscale Ag layer with minimal interdiffusion or reaction with W and Cu.
An Ag layer that is too thick or discontinuous may fail to produce the proposed improvement.
Formation of deleterious intermetallics during long-term thermal exposure or irradiation may eliminate the proposed benefits.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant thermal-conductivity increase, or degradation of mechanical performance or irradiation resistance beyond acceptable limits, would falsify the hypothesis.
